The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “found fault” in 1 of those places (33%), e.g. Mark 7:2. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 0% of the same verses.
The sense “found fault” is independently listed by Dodson, the KJV glosses, corroborating the corpus evidence.

prose.def: To find fault with someone or something, blaming or criticizing them for a shortcoming.
prose.article: μέμφομαι means to blame, criticize, or find fault, and all three of its New Testament uses point to that single core idea even though the translations are worded differently ("found fault," "God find fault," "fault"). It's a common everyday word in the papyri: one letter complains "I blame you greatly for the loss of two pigs," and another says "I blame the person who told you," showing how ordinary the term was. In the Septuagint it appears only a handful of times (Sirach 11:7, 41:7, and 2 Maccabees 2:7).
prose.caution: This word is rare, appearing only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament (2 in the critical text), so its measured range rests on thin evidence.

prose.def: A person who habitually complains about their lot in life, grumbling and discontented with their circumstances.
prose.article: This adjective describes someone who finds fault with their fate or lot, the grumbler who is never satisfied. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:16, where the Majority Standard Bible and BSB both render the surrounding phrase the same way. The word is built from μέμφομαι (to blame) plus μοῖρα (fate, lot), and Moulton-Milligan notes a related form ἀμεμψιμοίρητος ('blameless') in a papyrus from 164 B.C.; the term also turns up meaning 'censorious' in the astrologer Vettius Valens.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise range rests on slim evidence supplemented by a few outside attestations.
